# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

NELL was herding the cattle back from the rear field using Linger Lane. It was an evening in September, and ruby sunset light flooded every clearing and gap throughout the forest. Although that glow speckled the lane in places, it was mostly rather dark under the maples by then, while a translucent violet twilight, resembling airy wine, occupied the areas beneath the firs. Gales moved through their upper branches, and no melody on earth exceeds the sweetness of the wind's evening song among the fir trees.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0000 }

The cattle ambled calmly along the path, with Nell trailing behind them in a daze, reciting out loud the fight section of Marmion—a poem that had likewise formed a portion of their English studies the previous winter and which Miss Thorne had compelled them to memorize completely—and taking delight in its swift verses and the colliding lances within its descriptions. As she reached the verse
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0001 }

The unyielding spear-bearers continued to hold fast Their shadowy, unbreachable forest,
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0002 }

She paused in rapture, closing her eyes so she could more easily imagine being part of that valiant circle. Reopening them, she saw Isolde emerging from the gateway to the Pembroke field, carrying an air of such significance that Nell immediately sensed information was about to be shared. Nevertheless, she refused to show an excessively keen inquisitive nature.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0003 }

“Doesn’t this night resemble a purple dream, Isolde? Being alive fills me with such joy because of it. Mornings always seem superior to me when they arrive; yet the arrival of night makes me consider it even more beautiful.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0004 }

“The evening is exceptionally lovely,” Isolde remarked, “yet oh, Nell, I possess such news. Make a guess. Three attempts are allowed to you.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0005 }

“After all, Charlotte Pettigrew will be wed in the church, and Mrs. Wace desires that we adorn it,” exclaimed Nell.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0006 }

“It is a no. Charlotte’s sweetheart refuses to consent to it, given that not a single person has been wed in the church up to now, and he believes it would feel excessively similar to a burial service. This is such a shame, since it would offer so much enjoyment. Try another guess.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0007 }

“Will Odette’s mother allow her to hold a birthday party?”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0008 }

Isolde gave her head a shake, her dark eyes sparkling with amusement.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0009 }

“I cannot imagine what the cause might be,” Nell uttered in utter desperation, “if it is not that you were escorted back from the prayer meeting by Elias Purdy MacKinnon yesterday evening. Was that the case?”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0010 }

“I should certainly think not,” Isolde cried out with indignation. “If he had, I would hardly be prone to brag about it, that terrible creature! I was certain it was beyond your guessing. Mother received a missive from Aunt Lavinia today, in which Aunt Lavinia requests that you and I travel to town this coming Tuesday and remain at her place for the Exhibition. So there!”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0011 }

“Oh, Isolde,” Nell breathed softly, needing to rest against a maple tree to hold herself up, “are you truly being serious? Even so, I fear Thirza will forbid my going. She is bound to claim that she must not foster wandering around. She uttered those exact words just last week after Odette asked me to join them in their double-seated buggy for the American concert held at the Pale Sands Hotel. My desire was to attend, yet Thirza insisted that mastering my lessons at home was a wiser choice for me, as well as for Odette. It was a bitter disappointment to me, Isolde. My heart felt so completely broken that I refused to offer my prayers upon going to bed. However, feeling remorse for doing that, I arose during the middle of the night and recited them.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0012 }

“I’ll tell you,” Isolde said, “we’ll have Mother ask Thirza. You stand a better chance of being allowed to go if she does that; and should she agree, Nell, we will have a wonderful time. Having never attended an Exhibition myself, listening to the other girls discuss their visits is extremely frustrating. Odette and Opal have already gone two times, and they are visiting once more this year.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0013 }

“Until I discover if my going is possible or not, I will refuse to consider it whatsoever,” Nell declared with determination. “Should I dwell on it and then face disappointment, I could not endure it. However, if I end up going, I am extremely pleased that my new coat is going to be ready before then. Thirza was of the opinion that a new coat was unnecessary for me. Her view was that my former coat was perfectly adequate for one more winter and that a new dress should content me. Isolde, the dress is exceptionally pretty—it is navy blue and crafted in such a fashionable style. These days, Thirza continuously crafts my dresses in a stylish manner, since she stated she has no intention of allowing Obed to visit Mrs. Sowerby to get them made. That makes me so happy. Being virtuous becomes considerably simpler when your attire is stylish. For me, at any rate, it is simpler. I imagine that for people who are inherently good, it does not matter as much. Nevertheless, Obed insisted that I required a new coat, which led Thirza to purchase a gorgeous length of blue broadcloth, and an actual dressmaker over in Delford is currently tailoring it. Its completion is scheduled for Saturday evening, and I am attempting to avoid picturing myself strolling down the church aisle this Sunday wearing my new suit and cap, as I fear envisioning those matters is improper. Yet, it constantly creeps into my thoughts regardless of my efforts. The cap I have is exceedingly pretty. Obed purchased it for me on the day we went over to Delford. It happens to be a small blue velvet type that is currently so trendy, featuring gold cord and tassels. Isolde, your new hat is splendid and suits you so well. Seeing you enter the church this past Sunday filled my heart with immense pride because you are my closest friend. Do you think that pondering our garments to this extent is improper? According to Thirza, it is immensely sinful. Still, it is a remarkably fascinating topic, wouldn't you agree?”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0014 }

Thirza gave her consent for Nell to travel to town, and plans were made for Mr. Pembroke to drive the girls there on the coming Tuesday. Because Port Marlow lay at a distance of thirty miles and Mr. Pembroke intended to complete the round trip within a single day, setting off extremely early was required. However, Nell considered the entire experience a delight, arising prior to dawn on Tuesday morning. Looking out from her window, she felt certain the weather would remain pleasant, since the eastern sky over the firs of the Whispering Wood appeared entirely clear and silvery. Via the opening among the trees, a illumination glowed in the western gable of Pear Hill, signaling that Isolde had likewise risen.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0015 }

By the time Obed possessed the fire, Nell had put on her clothes, and she had prepared the morning meal when Thirza descended, although she herself felt far too agitated to consume food. Following the morning meal, the stylish fresh jacket and cap were put on, and Nell hurried across the stream and upward via the fir trees toward Pear Hill. Mr. Pembroke and Isolde were expecting her, and before long they were traveling on the road.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0016 }

Although the journey was lengthy, Nell and Isolde savored every moment. Traveling briskly along the damp roads proved enchanting in the early crimson morning light spreading over the harvested fields. The air possessed a cool freshness, while small, pale-blue vapors twisted through the lowlands and drifted away from the heights. Now and then, the path traversed forests where maples started displaying bright red foliage; now and then, it traversed streams over bridges that caused Nell’s flesh to shudder with that familiar, partly pleasurable terror; now and then, it meandered beside a haven coastline and traveled past a small group of weathered fishing cabins; at other times, it climbed to elevated grounds offering views of an expansive, arched landscape or a hazy blue sky; yet no matter where the route led, there was a great deal of fascinating things to talk about. The time was close to midday when they arrived in town and navigated to “Beechwood.” It proved to be a rather grand ancient residence, situated away from the road within the privacy of leafy elms and spreading beech trees. Miss Pembroke welcomed them at the entrance with a gleam in her keen dark eyes.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0017 }

“So you’ve finally come to visit me, you Nell-girl,” she remarked. “Goodness, child, what growth you’ve had! I do declare, you stand taller than me. Furthermore, you are far better-looking than you used to be as well. Though I expect you are already aware of that without anyone telling you.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0018 }

“I certainly did not,” Nell declared, her face beaming. “My freckles are fewer than they once were, which is a blessing in itself, yet I truly had not presumed to anticipate any further progress. Knowing you perceive another change pleases me immensely, Miss Pembroke.” The dwelling belonging to Miss Pembroke was appointed with “great magnificence,” which Nell later recounted to Thirza. Surrounded by such lavishness in the parlor, where Miss Pembroke had departed to attend to dinner, the pair of young country girls felt somewhat intimidated.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0019 }

“Doesn’t it resemble a palace?” Isolde murmured. “This is my first time inside Aunt Lavinia’s home, and its magnificence is completely unexpected. How I want Julia Bell to witness this—she acts so boastful regarding her mother’s parlor.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0020 }

“Velvet carpet,” Nell uttered with a luxurious sigh, “and silk curtains! Such things have been in my dreams, Isolde. But you know, I really do not think they make me feel terribly at ease. This room contains a vast quantity of items and each one is so grand that imagination has no room to play. Being poor brings one comfort at least—the number of things left to your imagination is so much greater.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0021 }

For years to come, Nell and Isolde used their stay in town as a reference point. It was filled with pleasures from beginning to end.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0022 }

Miss Pembroke escorted them to the Exhibition grounds on Wednesday, where she retained them for the entire day.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0023 }

“It was wonderful,” Nell recounted to Thirza afterwards. “I had no idea it would be so fascinating. It is hard to say which section I found most intriguing. My favorite parts were probably the horses, the flowers, and the handiwork. The top prize for knitted lace went to Flossie Tulk. That made me truly happy. Moreover, my own joy at her victory made me glad, because it demonstrates my growth as a person, doesn’t it, Thirza, since I can take pleasure in Flossie’s achievement? The runner-up prize for Gravenstein apples was awarded to Mr. Gorham Pullen, while Mr. Bell captured the top award for a pig. Isolde remarked that a Sunday-school superintendent winning an award for pigs struck her as absurd, though I fail to understand why. Don't you? According to her, she will be unable to forget it whenever he offers a serious prayer in the future. Clara Louise MacKinnon received an award for painting, whereas Mrs. Sowerby secured first prize for her homemade butter and cheese. Thus, Brierley achieved a strong showing, didn’t it? Mrs. Sowerby was present on that occasion, and seeing her well-known face amid that crowd of strangers made me realize the true extent of my affection for her. The attendance reached into the thousands, Thirza. The sheer size of the crowd made me feel terribly small. Furthermore, Miss Pembroke escorted us up to the grandstand so we could watch the horse races. Mrs. Sowerby declined to attend; claiming that horse racing was detestable, she felt that, as a church member, her moral obligation was to set a proper example by remaining behind. However, with so many attendees present, I doubt anyone would even notice Mrs. Sowerby’s absence. Even so, I probably shouldn't attend horse races frequently, as they possess an incredible allure. Isolde became so worked up that she tried to wager ten cents with me that the red horse would come out ahead. Though I doubted he would, I declined the bet, as I intended to relate all the details to Mrs. Wace, and I was certain that mentioning a wager to her would be inappropriate. Engaging in an action you cannot disclose to the minister's wife is invariably wrong. Having a minister's wife as a friend serves as a helpful second conscience. In the end, I was delighted that I refrained from betting, as the red horse actually won, which would have cost me ten cents. Hence, virtue proved to be its own compensation. We observed a man ascend in a balloon. Ascending in a balloon would be a dream of mine, Thirza; the experience would be immensely exciting; additionally, we spotted a man vending fortunes. Upon receiving ten cents, he had a tiny bird select a fortune for you. Miss Pembroke provided Isolde and me with ten cents apiece so we could have our fortunes drawn. My prediction stated that a wealthy, dark-complexioned man would become my husband, and my future home would be across the water. From that moment on, I observed every dark-complexioned man attentively, yet none of them particularly appealed to me, and regardless, I imagine it remains premature to be searching for him now. Ah, that day will stay in my memory forever, Thirza. Exhaustion kept me awake that night. True to her word, Miss Pembroke lodged us in the spare room. The accommodations were exquisite, Thirza, yet spending the night in a spare room lacks the magic I once imagined it held. Realizing that truth is the hardest aspect of aging, which I am starting to grasp. Upon finally obtaining the things you craved during childhood, they lose half their wonder.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0024 }

On Thursday, the girls went for a drive through the park, and later that evening, Miss Pembroke accompanied them to a concert at the Academy of Music to hear a famous prima donna perform. For Nell, the night unfolded as a radiant dream of pure joy.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0025 }

“Oh, Thirza, it exceeded any depiction I could give. You can imagine how extraordinary it was, considering I was so thrilled that speech failed me. Silence and pure rapture were all I could manage as I sat there. Madame Selitsky looked absolutely stunning, dressed in white satin and adorned with diamonds. However, the moment her singing commenced, every other thought vanished from my mind. Oh, describing my emotions is impossible. Yet, it gave me the impression that acting rightly would never be difficult again. My feelings mirrored those I experience while gazing at the stars. My eyes filled with tears, though, oh, those tears brought such joy. It brought me immense regret when the performance concluded, and I mentioned to Miss Pembroke that returning to an ordinary existence seemed impossible for me. She suggested that crossing the road to the restaurant for an ice cream might assist me. It struck me as quite unromantic; nevertheless, to my amazement, her idea proved effective. The ice cream tasted divine, Thirza, and partaking in it at eleven o’clock at night felt wonderfully thrilling and reckless. Isolde expressed her belief that she was destined for a city existence. Miss Pembroke inquired about my own view, yet I replied that formulating my genuine thoughts would require very deep reflection. Consequently, I pondered the matter once I had retired to bed. A bed is the finest place for resolving such questions. Thus, Thirza, I arrived at the decision that a city existence was not my destiny, a fact which pleased me. Enjoying ice cream within luminous eateries at eleven o’clock at night is delightful on occasion; nonethless, as an everyday routine, I would prefer resting in the east gable at eleven, deeply sleeping, yet somehow sensing through my dreams that stars sparkled outdoors and that breezes moved through the fir trees beyond the stream. I expressed this to Miss Pembroke during breakfast the following morning, causing her to laugh. Miss Pembroke usually found amusement in whatever I uttered, even during my most serious statements. I doubt that I enjoyed that reaction, Thirza, given that humor was not my intention. Still, she proves to be an exceptionally welcoming lady who provided us with splendid entertainment.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0026 }

When Friday arrived, it was time to go home, so Mr. Pembroke came in his car to pick up the girls.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0027 }

“Well, I hope you’ve had a good time,” said Miss Pembroke, when she took her leave of them.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0028 }

“Truly we have,” Isolde remarked.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0029 }

“And what about you, Nell-girl?”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0030 }

“Every minute of the time has been enjoyable to me,” Nell stated, flinging her arms around the neck of the old woman on an impulse and planting a kiss on her cheek that was wrinkled. Doing such a thing was something Isolde never would have ventured, and Nell’s liberty left her feeling somewhat horrified. Miss Pembroke was delighted, however, and from her veranda where she remained standing, she observed the buggy until it disappeared. Afterwards, she returned to the inside of her large home while uttering a sigh. Without those young, fresh lives, the place appeared exceedingly solitary. To speak truthfully, Miss Pembroke was an old lady who was somewhat self-centered, having rarely held affection for anyone other than herself. She prized individuals solely to the extent that they proved useful to her or provided her with entertainment. Entertainment had been supplied to her by Nell, who as a result held a favorable position in the old lady’s esteem. Nevertheless, Miss Pembroke caught herself reflecting not so much on the quaint speeches of Nell as on her fresh enthusiasms, her transparent emotions, her little winning ways, alongside the sweetness belonging to her eyes and lips.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0031 }

“Upon hearing that Thirza Abernethy had taken a girl from an orphan asylum, I considered her an old fool,” she reflected internally, “yet I suppose she did not commit a great error in the end. Had I a youngster such as Nell residing with me permanently, I would turn into a finer and more contented woman.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0032 }

The trip back proved just as enjoyable for Nell and Isolde as the journey there—even more so, in fact, because of the wonderful knowledge that home was awaiting them at its conclusion. As they drove through Pale Sands and made the turn onto the coastal route, the sun was setting. In the distance, the Brierley hills emerged dark against a sky of saffron. In the opposite direction, the moon ascended from the ocean, which became completely luminous and transformed under her glow. Each small cove following the winding street presented a wonder of moving ripples. Beneath them, the waves crashed with a gentle swish against the stones, and the crisp, invigorating breeze carried the scent of the ocean.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0033 }

“Oh, but it feels wonderful to be living and heading back home,” whispered Nell.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0034 }

As she traversed the log bridge spanning the brook, the kitchen illumination at Grey Shutters blinked a hospitable greeting to her upon her return, and via the unclosed doorway, the hearth fire gleamed, casting its cozy crimson radiance across the brisk fall evening. Nell hurried cheerfully up the slope and entered the kitchen, inside which a warm evening meal was set upon the table.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0035 }

“So you’ve returned?” said Thirza, putting away her knitting.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0036 }

“Yes, and oh, coming back feels wonderful,” Nell stated happily. “Everything, down to the clock, is something I could kiss. A broiled chicken, Thirza! Is it possible that you prepared that especially for me!”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0037 }

“Indeed, I did,” Thirza answered. “It occurred to me that a long drive like that would make you hungry for a truly delicious meal. Quickly remove your coat and hat, and we will eat our evening meal the moment Obed arrives inside. I am certainly relieved you are home, I have to admit. Being here without you has been terribly lonely, and I have never experienced four days that felt more drawn out.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0038 }

When supper was finished, Nell placed herself in front of the hearth in the space between Obed and Thirza, providing them with an extensive report regarding her trip.
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0039 }

“I have enjoyed myself immensely,” she ended with joy, “and I am certain this signifies a milestone in my existence. However, returning home was the finest part of everything.”
{: #nw-v01-c29-p0040 }
